title: CONCUBINE OR WIFE: What Was the Difference in the Biblical World?
paragraphs: CONCUBINE OR WIFE: What Was the Difference in the Biblical World?

The Bible mentions wives, concubines, multiple marriages, broken households, jealous women, wounded children, kings with harems, and families that look nothing like the picture-perfect homes we imagine when we hear the word “biblical.” But Scripture’s willingness to record something does not mean God is endorsing it. And once you understand the difference between a wife and a concubine, some of the Bible’s most troubling stories begin revealing something much bigger: what human beings did with marriage after Eden—and what Jesus came to restore.
There is a woman standing in the pages of Scripture whose title can make modern readers uncomfortable.
She is not called a prostitute.
She is not simply called a mistress.
She is not always treated as an unmarried sexual partner.
She is called a concubine.
And if you read that word through twenty-first-century eyes, you can completely misunderstand what the Bible is telling you.
Because in the biblical world, the difference between a wife and a concubine was not simply the difference between “married” and “unmarried.”
It was largely a difference of status, protection, household position, and rights.
And that distinction matters.
More than you might imagine.
Because buried underneath this ancient question is a painfully modern one:
What happens when a human being is loved enough to be wanted…but not honored enough to be given the same place?
That question reaches far beyond ancient marriage.
Some people reading this know exactly what it feels like to be somebody’s second choice.
Wanted privately.
Ignored publicly.
Useful when needed.
Forgotten when inconvenient.
Close enough to give everything.
Never secure enough to know where you stand.
And suddenly an ancient Hebrew word begins sounding painfully familiar.
The ordinary Hebrew word frequently translated “woman” or “wife” is אִשָּׁה — ’ishshah.
Depending upon context, it can mean “woman” or “wife.”
But Scripture also uses another word:
פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pilegesh
Usually translated:
concubine.

A pilegesh was generally a woman in a recognized sexual and household relationship with a man, often functioning as a secondary wife, but without the same standing normally associated with the primary wife.
That is why calling a biblical concubine merely a “girlfriend” or “mistress” can be seriously misleading.
Consider one of Scripture’s darkest stories.
Judges 19 begins with a Levite who “took to him a concubine.”
Yet only moments later the narrative speaks of him as her husband and speaks of her father as his father-in-law.
That detail matters.
The woman was called his concubine, yet the relationship carried recognized familial language.
She belonged within a marital household.
But she did not necessarily possess the status of a primary wife.
And Judges 19 eventually becomes horrifying.
The woman is abused, violated and dies in one of the bleakest episodes in the Old Testament.
The Bible does not beautify what happened.
It makes us look at it.
And the larger literary setting is impossible to miss:
“In those days there was no king in Israel.”
Judges repeatedly describes a society collapsing morally, where people increasingly do what is right in their own eyes.
So when someone reads Judges 19 and says, “Look what the Bible approves,” they have misunderstood how biblical narrative works.
Scripture sometimes tells you what humanity did precisely so you can see how desperately humanity needed redemption.
Description is not automatically prescription.
The Bible records murder.
That does not make murder holy.
It records adultery.
That does not sanctify adultery.
It records idolatry.
That does not endorse idols.
And it records polygamy and concubinage without asking us to pretend that the resulting households were Eden.
Look closely at those households.
Abraham.
Sarah.
Hagar.
Jacob.
Leah.
Rachel.
Bilhah.
Zilpah.
David.
Solomon.
Again and again, complicated sexual and marital arrangements are followed by jealousy, rivalry, political intrigue, wounded relationships, inheritance conflicts or family catastrophe.
Not every tragedy can simply be blamed on concubinage or polygamy.
Scripture is more sophisticated than that.
But neither should we miss the recurring brokenness.
Then there is Keturah.
And Keturah makes simplistic definitions fall apart.
Genesis 25:1 says:
“Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah.”
The Hebrew uses the ordinary word associated with woman/wife:
אִשָּׁה — ’ishshah.
Yet 1 Chronicles 1:32 identifies Keturah as:
“Abraham’s concubine.”
How can the same woman be described using both categories?
Because our modern boxes do not map perfectly onto ancient household terminology.
“Concubine” could describe a woman occupying a secondary marital status rather than merely describing an illicit sexual affair.
Genesis 25 makes another revealing distinction.
Abraham gives his principal inheritance to Isaac, while the sons of his concubines receive gifts and are sent away.
There it is.
Not necessarily the difference between relationship and no relationship.
The difference is standing.
Inheritance.
Household rank.
Security.
Status.
A concubine could bear children acknowledged as belonging to the father.
She could be attached to his household.
She could occupy a recognized relationship with him.
But she ordinarily stood beneath the primary wife in the household hierarchy.
That also helps explain why some women described elsewhere as servants or slave women could become involved in childbearing arrangements.
Hagar is perhaps the most famous example.
Sarah was barren.
In Genesis 16, she gave Hagar to Abraham.
And here we need to resist another temptation.
We should not romanticize ancient customs merely because biblical people practiced them.
Abraham was a man of extraordinary faith.
He was also a man capable of making disastrous decisions.
Sarah was a woman Scripture honors.
She was also human.
The heroes of Scripture need grace too.
That is one reason the Bible is so believable.
It does not airbrush its saints.
No carefully managed public-relations department would write Genesis the way Genesis is written.
No reputation-management consultant would tell Israel:
“Make sure everyone knows Jacob deceived his father.”
“Make sure everyone knows Judah slept with Tamar while believing she was a prostitute.”
“Make sure everyone knows David committed adultery and arranged a man’s death.”
“Make sure everyone knows Solomon accumulated wives until his heart was drawn away.”
But Scripture tells us.
Why?
Because the Bible is not ultimately the story of impressive people climbing toward God.
It is the story of a holy God pursuing fallen people who cannot rescue themselves.
And that changes how we read concubinage.
The existence of concubines in Scripture does not mean concubinage represents God’s highest design for marriage.
To discover the pattern, Jesus takes us backward.
Not to David.
Not to Solomon.
Not even to Abraham.
Back farther.
Back before kingdoms.
Before Israel.
Before sin shattered the human family.
Back to Eden.
Genesis 2:24 declares that a man leaves father and mother, holds fast to his wife, and they become one flesh.
When religious leaders questioned Jesus about marriage and divorce, Christ deliberately returned them to creation.
He spoke of the Creator making humanity male and female and of the two becoming one flesh.
Then Jesus said:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
Matthew 19:6.
Notice where Jesus grounds His answer.
Creation.
God’s intention.
Not every later accommodation produced by fallen human society.
Jesus distinguishes between what humanity was permitted within its hardness and what existed “from the beginning.”
That principle is enormous.
Because sometimes people ask the wrong question.
They ask:
“What could biblical people get away with?”
Jesus leads us toward a better question:
“What did God intend from the beginning?”
And those are not always the same thing.
Scripture can regulate life in a fallen society without declaring every feature of that society morally ideal.
The Law contains provisions protecting women, servants, foreigners, debtors and vulnerable people living inside social realities that were already broken.
Regulation is not necessarily celebration.
God meeting fallen humanity inside history should never be confused with God calling every human institution good.
And perhaps now this ancient study has moved uncomfortably close to home.
Because you may never have used the word pilegesh in your life.
But maybe you have lived with the wound behind it.
Maybe someone wanted your body without accepting responsibility for your soul.
Maybe someone promised commitment but kept you permanently uncertain.
Maybe you spent years trying to earn a position in somebody’s heart.
Maybe you accepted fragments because loneliness convinced you fragments were better than nothing.
Maybe you were betrayed by the person who promised covenant.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Maybe your marriage is barely breathing.
Maybe pornography quietly entered the space where intimacy used to live.
Maybe an emotional affair has already begun, although nobody has touched anybody yet.
Maybe you keep deleting messages because somewhere inside you, you already know.
Maybe you are sleeping beside somebody while feeling completely alone.
Maybe your family history is complicated enough that biblical stories about fractured households do not feel ancient at all.
And perhaps the hardest sentence in this entire article is this:
Knowing what broken people did in Scripture does not give us permission to baptize our own brokenness.
But neither does your brokenness place you beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
That is where the Gospel changes everything.
Jesus did not come merely to give humanity stricter relationship rules.
He came to rescue sinners.
Adulterers.
Liars.
The sexually broken.
The sexually exploited.
The abandoned.
The unfaithful.
The ashamed.
The self-righteous.
The people who destroyed their own homes.
And the people whose homes were destroyed by somebody else.
At the cross, Jesus did not die for a sanitized humanity.
He died for sinners.
And Scripture does not say, “Clean yourself until God can tolerate you.”
It calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
Repentance is not pretending the sin never happened.
Repentance is agreeing with God about it, turning from it, and coming to Christ for mercy and transformation.
Grace is not God announcing that sin never mattered.
Grace is God providing in Jesus what guilty people could never provide for themselves.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
A new heart.
A new identity.
A new direction.
And sometimes a long, painful process of restoration.
That is why the scandals in Scripture do not destroy Christianity.
They reveal why Christianity is necessary.
David needed grace.
Abraham needed grace.
Sarah needed grace.
Jacob needed grace.
Judah needed grace.
Solomon needed grace.
Peter needed grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
And grace has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe that is why this question about wives and concubines ultimately leads somewhere much greater than ancient household terminology.
The Bible is showing us what happens when human desire outruns divine design.
We create hierarchies where people get wounded.
We make promises and break them.
We use people.
We hide.
We rationalize.
We rename sin until it becomes easier to tolerate.
And then Jesus walks directly into the wreckage.
Not applauding it.
Not pretending it does not matter.
Redeeming people from it.
That distinction matters.
Christianity is not the announcement that everything you have done is acceptable.
Christianity is the announcement that Jesus Christ can save people who have done the unacceptable.
Maybe you have spent years thinking your scandal is the final chapter.
It isn't.
Maybe your sexual past makes you ashamed to pray.
Pray anyway.
Maybe your marriage failed.
Come to Christ.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Repent and come to Christ.
Maybe you were betrayed and now bitterness has become the only armor you trust.
Bring that wound to Christ.
Maybe nobody knows what you are doing behind the screen.
Christ does.
And His knowledge should terrify hypocrisy—but His mercy should give hope to the repentant.
You do not need another hiding place.
You need a Savior.
The woman reduced by society to a lower status mattered to God.
The wife crying behind a closed door matters to God.
The husband secretly fighting temptation matters to God.
The abandoned spouse matters to God.
The single person exhausted from waiting matters to God.
The person carrying sexual shame matters to God.
The child still suffering from the consequences of adults who could not remain faithful matters to God.
Jesus sees people whom societies turn into categories.
Wife.
Concubine.
Widow.
Adulterer.
Outcast.
Sinner.
Failure.
Jesus sees the person.
And the Gospel does something astonishing.
It does not merely improve your label.
It gives you a new identity in Christ.
Forgiven.
Reconciled.
Redeemed.
Made new.
Beloved by grace.
That does not erase earthly consequences.
Grace is not amnesia.
Some relationships cannot simply return to what they were.
Some trust must be rebuilt slowly.
Some wounds require years of healing.
Some consequences remain.
But consequences do not get the final word over everyone who belongs to Jesus.
Christ does.
So perhaps the deepest lesson behind the difference between a wife and a concubine is not merely historical.
It is this:
Human beings have always created degrees of belonging.
Jesus offers something radically different.
He does not invite repentant sinners into His Kingdom as tolerated spiritual concubines—close enough to serve Him but permanently kept outside the family because of their past.
Through Christ, believers are brought near.
The New Testament speaks with astonishing language about adoption, inheritance, reconciliation and belonging.
Not because we deserved a place.
Because Christ purchased our redemption.
That is grace.
You came carrying scandal.
Jesus offers redemption.
You came carrying guilt.
Jesus offers forgiveness.
You came carrying chains.
Jesus offers freedom.
You came believing your worst chapter had already named you.
Then Christ picked up the pen.
That is not permission to keep sinning.
It is the miracle that repentance does not end at condemnation when you run to Jesus.
So be honest before God today.
Not tomorrow.
Today.
If there is somebody you need to stop using, stop.
If there is an affair you need to end, end it.
If there is hidden sexual sin you need to confess, bring it into the light and seek faithful biblical accountability.
If you have wounded your spouse, do not demand instant trust because you apologized. Repentance bears fruit.
If someone wounded you, remember that forgiveness and reconciliation are related but not identical; rebuilding trust requires truth, wisdom and, where appropriate, safety and accountability.
And if you have spent years believing God could forgive everybody except you, look again at the cross.
Jesus did not bleed for imaginary sinners.
He died for real ones.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your private life. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Sometimes three words are enough to tell another believer, “I am still here. I am still fighting. Please stand with me.”
Somebody may think sexual failure has disqualified them forever. Somebody may be one honest encounter with the Gospel away from finally coming home.
It cannot.
It does not.
We never want money to occupy the place that belongs to Christ alone.
But voluntary Christian generosity can help Gospel work continue.
Your monthly support helps us keep going.

And when believers voluntarily use what God has entrusted to them to help biblical truth travel farther, that generosity can become an act offered for the glory of God—not because God needs our money, but because we want our resources to serve His purposes.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Pray.
Because sometimes the post you almost did not share becomes the post somebody reads alone at 2:00 in the morning when their life is falling apart.
Sometimes a sentence reaches a person you will never meet.
Sometimes a Scripture you already knew becomes somebody else's first encounter with hope.
And sometimes God allows ordinary believers to participate in extraordinary things simply because they were willing to say:
“Jesus, use what I have.”
The biblical world knew wives and concubines, primary households and secondary status, inheritance and exclusion, covenant faithfulness and devastating human failure.
But the Gospel brings us to something greater than all of it.
A Savior who knows exactly what we have done.
A cross sufficient for sinners.
An empty tomb announcing that death does not get the last word.
A King who does not merely cover scandal with religious language.
He transforms repentant sinners by grace.
So remember this when your past whispers your old name.
Remember it when shame drags out evidence from chapters God has already confronted.
Remember it when somebody decides that your worst moment is the only thing worth knowing about you.
Remember it when you are tempted to return to what Christ is calling you to leave behind.
Your scandal may explain where Jesus found you—but it does not have the authority to decide where His grace will take you.
